extracted.intended_audience: online instructors, course designers, and higher-education teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating and assessing 'teaching presence' in online learning: course design/organization, facilitation of discourse, direct instruction, assessment practices, tools, and teacher qualities. Focused on higher-education and formal online courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three components of teaching presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching presence consists of three major components: design and organization, facilitating discourse, and direct instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three interrelated functions as the organizing framework for evaluating an instructor's online role and for planning course activities; they are fundamental to teaching effectiveness in online and classroom instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and organization (course design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and organization includes building curriculum materials, repurposing materials (lecture notes, mini-lectures, commentaries), sequencing learning activities, negotiating timelines for group activities and projects, and encapsulating content as learning objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create high-quality, interactive resources (or reuse formalized learning objects), provide clear timelines, and model course structure so students perceive a consistent teaching presence; anticipate use of repositories (e.g., MERLOT, OCW) and standards for metadata/learning-object description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting the media/pacing mix right
rubrics_metrics.description: Select an appropriate mix of synchronous, asynchronous, and independent-study activities that balance the capacities of media to support social and cognitive presence with learning objectives, costs, access, and training requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh trade-offs: synchronous activities offer immediacy and familiarity but constrain time; asynchronous supports flexibility but may reduce coordination and 'in sync' feeling. Consider optional synchronous sessions, canned/streamed versions, and blended combinations tailored to student preferences and institutional capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personalized/conversational writing style to build presence
rubrics_metrics.description: A personalised, conversational (as opposed to academic) writing style—illustrating content with personal reflections, anecdotes, and the teacher’s own struggles and successes—helps learners identify with the teacher and can be inspirational and motivating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ teacher commentaries, mini-lectures, and personal insights where appropriate to establish rapport and convey enthusiasm; balance informality with academic expectations depending on assignment type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating discourse (trust and safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitating discourse requires developing a sense of trust and safety within the electronic community so learners feel comfortable posting thoughts and comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use introductory posts where students share specific information (model an answer yourself), icebreakers, and early synchronous activities to build social presence; address technical/social inhibitors to participation early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating critical discourse (structure and roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote critical (not merely conversational) discourse through well-structured learning activities with clearly defined roles for teachers and students and methods for assessing participation that reflect the effort of critical discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on teacher-initiated prompts; encourage student-led moderation and design activities that require students to formulate questions, challenge ideas, synthesize responses, and surface misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage student moderators and distributed leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion groups led by student moderators often increase participation, motivation, and satisfaction, though students may need role-modelling and support to moderate effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model moderation initially, provide explicit instructions and scaffolded roles, and evaluate moderation skills as part of participation assessment when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment clarity and explicit criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective teaching presence demands explicit and detailed discussion of the criteria by which student learning will be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make requirements and grading schemes transparent (e.g., weighting of participation), provide timely feedback, and align assessment with the process-oriented goals of social/constructivist learning when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and immediacy of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely and detailed feedback provided throughout and as near as possible to the performance of the assessed behaviour is most effective for motivation and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the advantages of rapid online feedback with realistic teacher workloads by setting and adhering to appropriate timelines; avoid fostering expectations of 24/7 instantaneous responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation weighting and incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in online activities is commonly assessed and weighted (often 10–25% of final mark) to incentivize contribution and community creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a participation weight that reflects the course's learning goals and student time constraints; be explicit about what is counted as participation (quality, quantity, timeliness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levine's discussion participation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Levine's posted expectations: instructor starts each weekly discussion; discussion window set (e.g., Sunday to following Sunday); focus on posted questions but bring related material; post at least two substantive messages per discussion question; postings should reflect understanding of course material and advance group negotiation of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Levine's combination of quantitative (two substantive postings) and qualitative guidance to make expectations explicit; provide examples of 'substantive' contributions and model them early in the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dabbagh's posting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Dabbagh recommends: distribute postings evenly during the discussion period; postings 1–2 short paragraphs; avoid 'I agree' style posts—explain why and support with readings/examples; address the questions; use quotes with page numbers; build on others' responses; bring related prior knowledge; use proper etiquette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce standards that balance frequency, length, engagement with readings, thread-building, and etiquette; adapt strictness to learners' language proficiency and course level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dabbagh evaluation criteria (Table 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three rubric dimensions for weekly message assessment: (1) Timely discussion contributions — e.g., Excellent: 5–6 postings well distributed through the week; (2) Responsiveness to discussion and demonstration of knowledge and understanding gained from assigned reading — e.g., Excellent: very clear that readings were understood and incorporated well into responses; (3) Adherence to online protocols — e.g., Excellent: all online protocols followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring bands provided (Excellent/Good/Average/Poor) with point allocations (e.g., 9–10, 8, 6–7, 5 or less). Use these explicit descriptors to operationalize grading of quantity, quality, and adherence to protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LMS/tools to support assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: An exemplary online learning system should provide teacher agents/tools to scan postings for spelling/grammar, total words, display thread context, graph posting dates, present a grade book, auto-mark objective items, and alert students of grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage available system features to reduce teacher workload and to provide rapid, structured assessment data; design rubrics that can be partially automated where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective/self-assessment using postings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use students' own postings as the basis for assessment by requiring an end-of-course reflection piece in which students quote their postings as evidence of contributions and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit guidance on how to extract representative quotations; this shifts responsibility toward students, saves teacher time, and promotes metacognition. Note that non-participants will struggle with this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting timelines and teacher time management
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must set and adhere to appropriate timelines to manage student expectations and avoid being consumed by the immediacy of online activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate response windows, office-hours-equivalents, and grading turnaround times; be 'ruthless' about guarding against constant checking and unrealistic availability demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salmon's e-moderator staged model
rubrics_metrics.description: Salmon's five-stage model for e-moderation: (1) access and motivation, (2) online socialization, (3) information exchange, (4) knowledge construction, (5) development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stages as a planning tool to sequence tasks and supports for learners, but customize the pace and emphasis to the cohort's technical/social experience; do not apply prescriptively when students already possess requisite skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an effective e-teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: An excellent e-teacher is first an excellent teacher (knowledgeable, enthusiastic, pedagogically skilled), has sufficient technical skills and internet efficacy to function, and demonstrates resilience, innovativeness, and perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or develop both pedagogical and basic technical competencies; provide supports or training where technical efficacy is low; encourage perseverance during adoption of new tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment adaptations for blogs and reflective formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Blog forms of discourse call for rubrics that pay greater attention to reflective learning and the diary-like, reflective origins of blogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing blogs, emphasize reflection, evidence of learning over time, and integration of personal insights; consult exemplar blog rubrics (e.g., Bowling Green State University collection) and adapt criteria accordingly.
